outcome: A May 2026 preprint by Suchanda Roy and Ramesh Hariharasubramanian ('Characterization of Word-Representable Near-Triangulations', arXiv:2605.25733) claims a complete forbidden-induced-subgraph characterization of word-representability for near-triangulations in general (not restricted to K4-free graphs), which would resolve the case this bullet names as open. It has not yet been digested by any expert, journal, or survey.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet (posed by the 2016 paper 'Colourability and word-representability of near-triangulations', arXiv:1605.01688, which characterised K4-free near-triangulations and left near-triangulations containing K4 as open, since K4 is non-3-colourable and the colouring-based approach used for the K4-free case does not apply) is squarely addressed by arXiv:2605.25733 (submitted 25 May 2026, single version, no later revisions or errata visible on arXiv). Its abstract states the paper gives 'a complete characterization of word-representable near-triangulations in terms of forbidden induced subgraphs' that 'unifies and extends the previously known characterizations for [polyomino triangulations, K4-free near-triangulations, face subdivisions of triangular grid graphs, triangulations of grid-covered cylinder graphs, and chordal near-triangulations], while also correcting inaccuracies appearing in earlier works.' The main result, Theorem 16 in the fetched HTML rendering, is stated for general near-triangulations ('Let G be a near-triangulation. Then G is word-representable if and only if it contains none of the graphs from Figure 8 as an induced subgraph'), with no K4-free restriction, so on its face it covers the K4-containing case this bullet asks about. I was not able to render the full PDF body (only metadata and an incompletely-decoded content stream came through two separate fetch attempts), so I could not independently verify the forbidden-subgraph list in Figure 8 or check the proof of Theorem 16 line by line; my reading of the theorem statement rests on an automated HTML extraction rather than my own read of the typeset proof. No journal listing, conference abstract, citing paper, or expert commentary (blog, Mathoverflow, Kitaev's own subsequent papers) discusses this specific preprint yet — it is four months old at the time of this research and appears to be genuinely unreviewed. A site called pith.science hosts an AI-generated review of the paper, but that is third-party automated commentary on the paper, not an expert digestion, and in any case I could not retrieve its actual review text (the fetch returned empty content twice). No acknowledgements section, methods statement, or any language anywhere in the paper, its arXiv listing, or secondary discussion indicates any AI system was used by the authors in producing the characterization or its proof; this appears to be ordinary human graph-theory research. Given a single, very recent, unreviewed preprint with a claim that (on its stated theorem) resolves the open case, I classify this as 'claimed' rather than 'resolved', with resolution_direction 'confirmed' since the claimed result answers the characterization question rather than refuting the possibility of a clean characterization.
competing_reading: It is conceivable that Theorem 16's forbidden-subgraph list, despite being stated for 'near-triangulations' unqualified, is only actually verified/proved by the authors for the K4-free and previously-studied subclasses being unified, with the K4-containing extension resting on a gap or an implicit assumption not visible in the metadata-level extraction I obtained. Because I could not read the full proof (only the theorem statement, via an automated HTML-to-text extraction rather than my own direct read of the source), I cannot rule out that the 'K4-containing' generalization is weaker than the abstract suggests, e.g. restricted to a specific K4-containing subclass rather than fully general. If so, the correct status would still be 'partial' rather than 'claimed' for the full open problem, and 'claimed' for a case of it.
what_would_settle_it: A direct read of the full typeset PDF (Sections stating and proving Theorem 16 and the definition/enumeration of Figure 8's forbidden subgraphs), or an expert digestion (journal referee report, citing survey, or a specialist's blog/MathOverflow commentary) confirming the theorem's scope explicitly includes near-triangulations containing K4 as an induced subgraph, not just the previously-solved K4-free and named subclasses.
